subtopics.title: Iran-Israel Rivalry and the Axis of Resistance
subtopics.summary: Iran and Israel were allies during the Shah's reign, but relations turned hostile after the 1979 revolution, when the new Islamic government broke all ties with Israel. The Revolutionary Guard Corps then built a network of armed groups called the Axis of Resistance to confront Israel and its rivals. Its members include Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and Ansar Allah (Houthis) in Yemen.
facts: Iran and Israel were allies during the reign of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
The Shah was ousted in 1979 and an Islamic State was established in Iran.
The Khomeini government broke all relations with Israel after 1979.
The Shah ordered Khomeini to leave Iran in 1964; Khomeini then led the revolution from Iraq.
Khomeini called America the 'Big Devil' and Israel the 'Little Devil'.
The IRGC created the Axis of Resistance, a network of armed groups.
Hezbollah (Lebanon) was formed to fight Israeli forces that had invaded Lebanon in 1982.
Hamas (Gaza City) is linked to the outbreak of the First Intifada against Israel.
Ansar Allah emerged in Yemen as an opposition movement against President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Iran supports the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon as pressure fronts against Israel.

subtopics.title: Strait of Hormuz and Global Energy Shock
subtopics.summary: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is the only maritime outlet for the Gulf's oil and gas exports. The booklet warns that a blockade could push Brent crude prices up and possibly trigger a global energy crisis. Speculative demand from a risk premium can raise prices even before any supply is actually lost.
facts: The strait lies between Iran (north) and the Musandam Peninsula of Oman (south).
It connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and further to the Arabian Sea.
It is the only maritime outlet for the Persian Gulf's oil and gas exports.
It carries nearly 20% of global oil supply.
About 1/5 of global LNG trade and 1/3 of global fertiliser exports transit this corridor.
Traders add a risk premium, which can create artificial price rises through speculative demand.
Conflict could spill into the Red Sea or Suez Canal, raising transit times and freight costs.
India imports about 85% of its crude oil.
Each $1 rise in oil price adds about $1.5 billion a year to India's import bill.
Nearly 40% of India's crude oil imports and over 80% of its LPG imports pass through the strait.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Talks and Military Strikes
subtopics.summary: Nuclear talks in Geneva collapsed over US demands that Iran dismantle Fordow and Natanz and halt uranium enrichment. The joint offensive then used heavy bombers, including US B-2 bunker-buster strikes on Fordow. Iran responded with missiles, including the Sejjil, in strikes on Israeli and US military bases.
facts: The 2015 JCPOA was signed between Iran and the P5+1 group of countries.
Under the JCPOA, Iran agreed to limit uranium enrichment to 3.67%.
The US withdrew from the JCPOA unilaterally in 2018 and reinstated sanctions.
Geneva talks collapsed over US demands to dismantle Fordow and Natanz and halt enrichment.
US B-2 bombers used bunker-buster bombs to strike the fortified Fordow facility.
US airstrikes targeted Kharg Island, which handles nearly 90% of Iran's crude oil exports.
Iranian missiles struck near the heavily protected Dimona nuclear research centre.

The Sejjil is a two-stage, solid-fuel, medium-range ballistic missile.
The Sejjil is called the 'Dancing Missile' for its high-altitude manoeuvrability.

subtopics.title: Iran's Supreme Leader
subtopics.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei was named Iran's third Supreme Leader after Ali Khamenei was assassinated, the first hereditary-style transfer since the revolution. The office holds ultimate authority over Iran's political, military and religious institutions. The leader is chosen by the 88-member Assembly of Experts, and the office's authority derives from the doctrine of Velayat-e Faqih.
facts: Mojtaba Khamenei was named the third Supreme Leader after Ali Khamenei's assassination.
This was the first hereditary-style leadership transfer in Iran since the revolution.
The Supreme Leader is Iran's de jure head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

The Assembly of Experts is an 88-member clerical body elected by the public.
The Assembly of Experts elects the leader, supervises his performance and can remove him if unfit.

subtopics.title: India's Energy Security and Reserves
subtopics.summary: India imports about 85% of its crude oil, and a large share of its crude and LPG imports transit the Strait of Hormuz. Its Strategic Petroleum Reserves are meant to cushion supply shocks, with current storage of about 3.37 MMT against a total capacity of 5.33 MMT. The government invoked the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 to ensure LPG availability during the crisis.

quizzes.passage:
Diplomacy over Iran's nuclear programme had been a central source of tension in West Asia for years. Talks held in Geneva collapsed after the United States insisted that Iran take apart some of its main nuclear sites and stop enriching uranium altogether. The breakdown came against a longer history. A 2015 agreement between Iran and a group of major powers had limited Iran's enrichment in return for sanctions relief. The United States later walked away from that deal and reinstated sanctions, and Iran began to breach the limits it had accepted.

Tensions were also fuelled by concerns over the regional balance of power. Iran's effort to build a land corridor through Iraq, Syria and Lebanon alarmed Washington and its partners, while Iran's support for armed groups in several countries created pressure fronts against Israel.

When diplomacy failed, the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. The offensive relied on heavy bombers and targeted fortified installations, including nuclear infrastructure. Iran responded with missiles and drones aimed at Israeli and American military targets, and the retaliatory attacks reached several Gulf states. The escalation was the latest step in a long rivalry over influence in West Asia, and it raised fears of a wider conflict across the region.

quizzes.passage:
The nuclear dispute between Iran and Western powers had shaped regional politics for years. A deal signed in 2015 placed limits on Iran's nuclear activity in exchange for sanctions relief. Later, the United States left that agreement on its own and restored sanctions, and Iran began to go beyond the limits it had accepted.

Negotiations later took place in Geneva, but they broke down after Washington demanded major changes to Iran's nuclear facilities and a permanent halt to uranium enrichment. Iran's wider regional role also worried its rivals, including a network of allied armed groups spread across the Middle East.

When talks failed, the United States and Israel carried out joint strikes on Iran. The attacks used heavy bombers and targeted fortified sites. Iran responded with missiles and drones aimed at Israeli and American military targets, and the attacks reached several Gulf states. The escalation raised concerns about a wider war in West Asia and about the security of shipping routes in the region.

quizzes.passage:
Iran's political system is built around the office of Supreme Leader, which holds ultimate authority over the country's political, military and religious institutions. The office is the country's head of state in law and oversees national security and foreign policy. Its holder also has a strong say over who may stand in elections, through the vetting process.

The office rests on an idea that a senior Islamic jurist should exercise ultimate political authority in an Islamic state, combining religious legitimacy with political governance. The idea was given an institutional form after the 1979 revolution, when the first holder of the office took power.

The leader is chosen by a clerical body that is itself elected by the public. This body also monitors how the leader performs his duties. A 1989 constitutional amendment reshaped the rules for selecting the office's holder, and the office has recently passed to a new holder after the death of its previous occupant.

quizzes.passage:
Iran's Supreme Leader sits at the top of the country's political system and holds ultimate authority over its political, military and religious institutions. The office is head of state in law and commands the armed forces. Its holder also oversees national security and foreign policy, and has influence over the vetting of candidates for elections.

The office rests on a religious-political idea: that a senior Islamic jurist should hold ultimate political authority in an Islamic state. The idea was given institutional form after the 1979 revolution, when the first holder of the office took power.

The leader is chosen by a clerical body that is elected by the public. That body also monitors the leader's performance. A 1989 constitutional amendment changed the rules for choosing the office's holder, and the office has now passed to a new leader after the death of its predecessor.

quizzes.passage:
India depends heavily on imported energy, and much of its supply moves through the Strait of Hormuz, the passage that connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman. Because a large share of India's crude oil imports and a significant portion of its gas imports use this route, tensions in the region are felt quickly across the Indian economy.

Global crude oil prices have climbed sharply during the crisis, which raises the cost of India's import bill. Higher costs then feed into transport, fertiliser, manufacturing and logistics, adding pressure on inflation and on the government's finances, since it may absorb part of the price shock through tax cuts.

To cushion such shocks, India maintains a strategic petroleum reserve, meant to act as a buffer against global oil shocks and to help stabilise prices. Reserves of this kind are meant to ensure that industry and defence receive uninterrupted fuel during supply disruptions, and to reduce dependence on external suppliers. Many governments hold reserves covering a set period of net oil imports, and India's programme is part of its response to the current instability in West Asia.

quizzes.passage:
India is one of the world's largest energy importers, and most of its crude oil arrives by sea. A large part of that supply moves through the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway that links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman. Tensions in West Asia therefore pose a direct risk to India's energy supply.

Rising prices are a second concern. Global crude oil prices have climbed sharply during the crisis, which increases the cost of India's oil import bill. Higher costs then feed into transport, fertiliser, manufacturing and logistics, adding pressure on inflation and on the government's finances, since it may absorb part of the price shock through tax cuts.

India's strategic petroleum reserve is designed to act as a buffer against global oil shocks and to help stabilise prices. Reserves of this kind are meant to ensure that industry and defence receive uninterrupted fuel. Many governments hold reserves covering a set period of net oil imports, and India's own programme is part of its response to the current instability.
